entries.title: Germany face belgium in Nations League quarterfinals — Klopp plays down favorites tag
entries.summary: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.
entries.content:
November 20, 2026

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.

Germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals—after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.

"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.

"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."

Historical success for Germany against Belgium

The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.

Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.

Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway – a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.

In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.

The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

entries.title: EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
entries.summary: The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed on "landmark" deals on youth mobility and trade. Leaders on both sides praised the agreement as they seek to rebuild ties.
entries.content:
Europe

EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit

November 20, 2026

The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed on "landmark" deals on youth mobility and trade. Leaders on both sides praised the agreement as they seek to rebuild ties.

European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.

This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.

During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.

'A good day for Britain' and 'A good day for Europe'

"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.

Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.

He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."

Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."

'Brexit took opportunities from young people'

He went further and said "Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.

Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."

She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."

Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.

She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."

Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it."

In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.

"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.

What do the deals involve?

The three key agreements establish ways to:

  • Simplify food exports by reducing red tape
  • Link the UK and EU emissions-trading systems
  • Establish a youth experience scheme

The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.

No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students

"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.

Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,."

On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.

They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.

According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.

Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.

The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

How do Brits feel about Brexit now?

On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.

Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.

Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

entries.title: Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV
entries.summary: In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.
entries.content:
Turkey

Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV

November 20, 2026

In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.

Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.

A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.

The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing."

Accused of ties to the Gülen movement

The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.

According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.

A familiar pattern in Turkey

It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.

Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.

In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.

The opposition is being silenced

Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.

Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.

Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once."

Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.

'Black winter for press freedom'

The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.

"These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Africa at COP31: Will climate cash finally flow?
entries.summary: As the curtains draw to a close on COP31 in Antalya, one question looms large for African countries: will climate promises finally translate into the funding African communities need to cope with a warming world?
entries.content:
Africa

Africa at COP31: Will climate cash finally flow?

November 20, 2026

As the curtains draw to a close on COP31 in Antalya, one question looms large for African countries: will climate promises finally translate into the funding African communities need to cope with a warming world?

For millions across the continent, climate change is no longer an abstract environmental concern debated in conference halls. It is already reshaping daily life, livelihoods and even decisions about where people can live.

In Zimbabwe, Harare resident Tsitsi Moyo says the effects are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. "The extreme heat wave we have been experiencing I think also has issues to do with rainfall patterns."

Jane Okello has witnessed similar changes in Uganda, describing increasingly erratic weather, including periods of unusually heavy rainfall associated with El Nino.

Their experiences reflect a wider trend across the continent. Communities that depend on predictable seasons for agriculture, water supplies and income are finding it harder to plan for the future as weather patterns become more extreme and less reliable.

For some, the consequences go beyond disrupted harvests or shrinking water supplies. Climate pressures are also influencing migration patterns. According to Professor Alfred Ngomanda, Permanent Secretary of the Gabon Climate Council, environmental stress can push people to leave their homes in search of more favorable conditions and more secure livelihoods.

Climate change is rarely the sole reason people migrate. However, droughts, floods, declining agricultural output and other environmental strains often intensify existing economic and social challenges, making displacement more likely.

As African countries prepare to make their case at the climate negotiations, Ngomanda stressed that the continent must emphasize the global importance of its natural resources.

"We will go to Ethiopia to assert that the Congo Basin is a stabilizing element for the global climate, and not just for Africans."

Why climate finance matters

At the heart of the discussions at COP31 is climate finance, the funding used to help countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the impacts of climate change.

COP, or the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, brings together governments from around the world to negotiate action on global warming. The talks build on the Paris Agreement, adopted at COP21 in 2015, which aims to keep global temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees.

For African countries, the challenge is not simply making climate commitments, but securing the resources needed to turn those commitments into reality.

Opening the conference, United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres highlighted what he described as a fundamental injustice in the global response to climate change. "Developing countries face a double injustice: they bear the brunt of climate change but struggle to access the finance they urgently need," Guterres said.

The scale of the financing gap remains stark. According to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, the continent received about $52 billion (€44.5 billion) in climate finance in 2022, far short of its estimated annual requirement of $190 billion. Much of that funding also comes as loans, adding pressure to already strained public finances.

The shortfall is especially significant given that Africa contributes only about 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains one of the regions most vulnerable to climate change.

African governments are therefore calling for funding that is more predictable, accessible and affordable, particularly for programs intended to help communities adapt to extreme weather, strengthen resilience and protect livelihoods.

From commitments to action

African negotiators say the focus now must be on making sure that climate commitments produce tangible results on the ground. Speaking at a press conference on November 19, Veronica Nonhlanhla Jakarasi, lead negotiator for the African Group of Negotiators, argued that the continent needs a dedicated mechanism to translate climate proposals into funded projects.

"What we need is a mitigation implementation facility that moves Africa's proposals into actual financing and projects on the ground."

She said such a facility would help direct more resources to the continent while supporting economic growth, green industrialization and the development of Africa's critical minerals sector without driving up emissions.

Mitigation focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while adaptation involves preparing for and responding to climate impacts. African countries insist both are essential if the continent is to pursue development while coping with increasingly severe weather events.

Negotiations remain difficult. A revised COP31 draft circulated on November 19, removed references to phasing out fossil fuels and dropped a proposed annual adaptation-finance target of $120 billion. While talks are ongoing and the text does not represent a final agreement, the changes underscore the political and financial battles that still shape international climate action.

For women like Moyo and Okello, however, the significance of COP31 will ultimately be measured far from the conference venue. Climate finance can support drought-resistant farming, improved water management systems, early-warning networks and infrastructure intended to withstand floods and extreme heat. But pledges alone will not deliver those outcomes. Countries must be able to access the money, implement projects effectively, and ensure support reaches the communities that need it most.

Gerauds Wilfried Obangome contributed to this article

entries.title: Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over
entries.summary: The ICJ has held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Community members have hailed the ruling, but caution that achieving real change will be long and hard.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over

November 20, 2026

The ICJ has held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Community members have hailed the ruling, but caution that achieving real change will be long and hard.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community a decade ago, in a historic judgment hailed by the long-persecuted minority and rights groups.  

The United Nations' top court also ordered the Myanmar government to prevent a repeat of the crimes, undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya and provide the victims with reparations or, where it cannot, compensate them.

The judgment came seven years after The Gambia filed the case with the court, accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the country's predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017.

It is the ICJ's first finding of genocide against a state, and the first ruling in any of the cases filed against Myanmar or its leaders in multiple courts around the world.

How do Rohingya see the ruling?

Lucky Karim was 14 when she and her mother and brothers were forced to flee their village in Rakhine State to escape the Myanmar military's advance in August 2017.

She joined the roughly 700,000 other Rohingya who crossed the border into Bangladesh at the time.

Now a prominent Rohingya activist, Karim heard the court's judgment in person in The Hague.

"For me … it's a very personal day, a personal moment, as someone who survived and escaped genocide in 2017. It took nearly a decade for the world to finally hear our voice," she said.

"For generations the [Myanmar] military stripped away our identity, our citizenship, tried to erase us from our homeland, told the world that what they did to us in 2017 was merely clearance operations, or worse, that we didn't even exist," said Wai Wai Nu, another Rohingya activist and former political prisoner.

Today, she said, their decades of persecution "is actually validated, and the truth has come out."

Tun Khin, a Rohingya activist and plaintiff in a universal jurisdiction case against Myanmar in Argentina, called the judgment "a historic moment" and "a big day for the Rohingya."

The press bureau of the Myanmar president's office did not respond to DW's requests for comment. The government's main mouthpiece, the state-run New Light of Myanmar newspaper, made no mention of the ruling online.

'Far in excess of what was justified'

Throughout the trial, Myanmar claimed that its actions in Rakhine State were strictly part of legitimate counterinsurgency operations against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group in the area that had been attacking police and military posts.

The ICJ flatly rejected the argument. "The court views casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, reading from the 15-judge panel's 9-6 ruling in The Hague.

"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," he added.

A UN-backed fact-finding mission concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. By some estimates, about 1 in 5 of them were children.

Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin in Ireland, said the court's ruling was both historic and "monumental" not only because it found a state responsible for genocide, but also because "it demonstrates that establishing genocidal intent is not impossible."

He noted that the panel took pains to show that The Gambia's case passed the court's established "only reasonable inference" test for genocidal intent. The ruling also "helpfully affirms" that forced transfer, targeting children and sexual violence could be relevant factors, he added.

'Not conditions amenable to … relief'

Amid elation among the Rohingya and rights groups, the focus quickly turned to making the court's prescribed remedies real.

The ICJ said Myanmar was now obliged to allow the "safe, voluntary and dignified" return of those who fled, investigate the crimes, and prosecute those found responsible. It also told Myanmar to return or replace all stolen property or, within two years, show the court it was compensating victims for what it could not.

But those behind the genocide, including former military chief and current president, Min Aung Hlaing, have remained in power since toppling Myanmar's democratically elected government in 2021.

Much of the country, including Rakhine State, is still in the midst of a brutal civil war between the military and an array of armed resistance groups. And the group that now controls most of Rakhine, the Arakan Army, is widely accused of persecuting the Rohingya as well.

"These are not conditions amenable to realizing the relief ordered by the ICJ anytime soon," said Becker.

Enforcing the court's orders ultimately falls to the UN Security Council. But China and Russia, which both back the Myanmar government and keep it well armed, would "almost certainly" veto any proposed Council resolution that aims to punish Myanmar, said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group.

"Whatever pressure there is will come from governments and the General Assembly, not the Council," he said.

Immediately after Thursday's ICJ judgment, the UK said it was expelling Myanmar's defense attache in London and would call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the court's decision.

'This is just the beginning'

A number of Western governments have already buried Myanmar under round after round of sanctions over the past decade, but with little to no apparent effect.

Myanmar is even taking tentative steps to shake off its global pariah status and restore regular relations with the rest of the world. Min Aung Hlaing has been warmly hosted by eight Asian and Eastern European countries since arranging his transition from army general to president earlier this year following rigged elections.

Horsey said the ICJ judgment would slow those efforts but not reverse them.

"Most governments in the region will keep engaging, but those with Muslim-majority publics, especially Malaysia and Indonesia, will find it harder to justify at home," he said.

Japan and South Korea, which maintain extensive business ties with Myanmar, are likely to remain cautious, he added, while the United States, which has reportedly had recent meetings with senior government officials, would keep up a transactional relationship.

"For [Myanmar], the real cost is that every government that deals with it will now have to explain why it is engaging a state found responsible for genocide," Horsey said.

'They want to return home'

The Rohingya, meanwhile, expect a long and difficult fight for real change.

"A judgment in The Hague will not on its own stop the bombs or feed starving families or stop the atrocities in Rakhine State," said Wai Wai Nu. "It is imperative that the international community take action to enforce the ruling," she added.

Karim said other countries should use the ICJ judgment "as a tool to open every possible door to help us and protect the people on the ground."

The Gambia's lead counsel in the case, Arsalan Suleman, said the genocide ruling could be used to help hold the perpetrators to account in other courts. The International Criminal Court, for one, is weighing an arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity, also against the Rohingya.

Tun Khin said the wish of most Rohingya is simple, if still hard to foresee. "They want to return home, to their houses and own villages," he said, but this time with full citizenship rights and legal protection.

"It will take time," he acknowledged. "This is just the beginning."

entries.title: FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?
entries.summary: Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?
entries.content:
November 20, 2026

Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?

Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.

Gianni Infantino – the powerful incumbent

Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.

Philippe Diallo — Europe's principled alternative

Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.

He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.

"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."

Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.

Kozo Tashima — an underdog as a possible king maker?

The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.

During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.

"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.

"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.

But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.

"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he said.

"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.

However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.

If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

entries.title: Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched one of the largest aerial attacks since the invasion began. Poland has said its airspace was violated in the process. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says

Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched one of the largest aerial attacks since the invasion began. Poland has said its airspace was violated in the process. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Zelenskyy said the Russian attack included 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles
  • At least 8 people were killed and several bridges and energy facilities were hit
  • Poland said its airspace was violated during the Russian attack
  • France has called for a UN Security Council meeting in light of the attacks

Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:

Skip next section UK's Andy Burnham condemns Russian violation of Polish airspace

UK's Andy Burnham condemns Russian violation of Polish airspace

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Russia's violation of Polish airspace "utterly unacceptable."

"The incursion into ​Polish airspace is utterly unacceptable. I condemn it unreservedly," ​Burnham said at an EU-UK ​summit press conference ‌in Brussels.

The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the "Coalition of the Willing" that ​groups allies of Ukraine, including the UK.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the move was a Russian provocation aimed at dividing Europe.

"Europe ​will not be ‌deterred from our support for Ukraine," Streeting said. "We will not allow ⁠Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the ⁠frontline ​in Ukraine is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere."

Skip next section Moscow invites Germany, France and UK for talks on Ukraine — Russian media

Moscow invites Germany, France and UK for talks on Ukraine — Russian media

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has reportedly invited representatives from Germany, France and the UK to Moscow for talks on the war in Ukraine, according to Russian news agency Interfax.

"We are waiting for a reply," the diplomat was reported to have said.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said European officials would be invited to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

Interfax reported that Ryabkov stressed that such a visit would not automatically mean that European nations would be involved in the negotiations on ending the war on Ukraine.

A statement from the French president's office said Europeans were ready to visit Moscow if given a full role in Ukraine talks.

European leaders have been pushing for a seat at the negotiation table, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying on Thursday that the outcome of the war in Ukraine would determine European security for years to come.

Skip next section EU releases €7.9 billion to Ukraine

EU releases €7.9 billion to Ukraine

The European Commission said it has released another €7.9 billion ($8.67 billion) ‌to ⁠Ukraine to support the country's finances and keep public administration running.

"Ukraine continues to deliver on reforms, while defending itself each and every day. Today, we are disbursing nearly €8 billion — this is the largest payment made so far," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"This makes it clear: real progress on reforms brings real results and benefits. As Ukraine perseveres and moves further on its European path, they can count on our support," said von der Leyen.

It’s the ninth disbursement of funds under the mechanism to support Ukraine.

With today's release of funds, the EU and its member states have provided €245.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine, which includes €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.

Skip next section Germany says Polish airspace violation part of Moscow's 'ongoing provocations'

Germany says Polish airspace violation part of Moscow's 'ongoing provocations'

The German Foreign Ministry has expressed its support for Poland after reports a Russian missile had entered Polish airspace.

"Russian missiles have once again violated Polish airspace. This is part of Russia's ongoing provocations," Germany's Foreign Ministry said in a statement on X.

"Instead of signaling a willingness to negotiate, Putin is signaling the opposite: he is opting for confrontation," the post said.

"We stand firmly by our neighbor and NATO ally Poland," the statement concluded.

Skip next section NATO chief condemns 'grave violations' of Poland's airspace

NATO chief condemns 'grave violations' of Poland's airspace

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said he had spoken to Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk about what he called "grave violations of Polish airspace overnight."

Rutte said that NATO jets had been scrambled in response.

"We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend," Rutte said.

"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine," the NATO chief said.

"I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine," Rutte said.

Skip next section France calls for UN Security Council meeting after Russia's strikes

France calls for UN Security Council meeting after Russia's strikes

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said that Paris had requested a UN Security Council meeting after Russia launched one of the war's largest missile attacks on Ukraine.

"The Kremlin has struck Kyiv again. Civilians have been killed," Jean-Noel Barrot said on X.

"These are crimes. France condemns them in the strongest possible terms," Barrot said.

"I have requested a meeting of the United Nations Security Council. Russia will have to answer for its actions there," said France's top diplomat.

On Thursday at the Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Ukraine needed to be able to defend itself and that allies needed to ensure Kyiv had the means to do so.

Skip next section Estonia shutting border with Russia from December

Estonia shutting border with Russia from December

The government of Estonia said road border crossings with Russia would be shut from December 1 on security grounds.

"The closure ​of the border crossing points is not a reaction to a ​single incident, ‌but the next step following Russia's aggression against Ukraine and the increasing frequency of sabotage and hybrid operations in Europe," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement.

The Kremlin has denied the allegations saying they're part of a pattern of false allegations against Moscow originating from European countries.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Estonia of planning to erect a new "Iron Curtain" and said it would respond.

"Should Tallinn proceed with these ‌plans, our country will take the necessary ‌political ​and diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its national interests," Zakharova told a press briefing in Moscow.

Skip next section Ukraine says dozens of Russian oil and defense targets hit in past 50 days

Ukraine says dozens of Russian oil and defense targets hit in past 50 days

The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said that his forces had hit 40 Russian oil facilities and defense industry targets in the past 50 days.

Brovdi said via the Telegram that among those targets, five of them had been hit more than once.

He went on to say that ​the Dorogobuzh ​chemical plant ‌in Russia's Smolensk region was ​struck ⁠on November 10 ⁠and ​November 20.

Ukraine has managed to adapt on the battlefield with the use of drone technology which has allowed hundreds of drone sorties, in some cases deep inside Russian territory, on a daily basis.

Skip next section Zelenskyy says overnight Russian attacks 'one of the largest'

Zelenskyy says overnight Russian attacks 'one of the largest'

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was targeted by more than 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, 27 of which he said were ballistic missiles.

"The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives," Zelenskyy said in a detailed post on social media platform X.

Zelenskyy listed what had been hit during the overnight strikes

  • Energy facilities, substations and power lines, which Zelenskyy said nuclear facilities depended on
  • Logistics and bridges across the Dnipro, three were reportedly struck
  • Regular residential buildings damaged
  • Zelenskyy says Russians used missiles with cluster warheads and described it as "one of the largest attacks"

He accused Russia of carrying out second strikes on targets that had already been hit, in so-called "double-tap strikes."

"People had essentially already been killed by the time specialists were inspecting the initial damage to the facilities, as the Russians were carrying out double-tap strikes," Zelenskyy said.

Most Russian missiles reportedly intercepted

Zelenskyy said that in all 79 cruise missiles had been intercepted and that fighter jets had been scrambled to deal with the aerial threats involving F-16s, Mirages and MiGs.

"Ballistic missiles are, unfortunately, much more difficult to deal with, and that depends not on our capabilities but on the supply of missiles by our partners," Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine's leader called for a "clear response" from the global community.

It is important that our partners not only issue statements in support of Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also follow through on specific agreements on air defense," Zelenskyy said.

He pointed out the timing of the latest attacks and said Putin launched them "in a highly demonstrative manner – following weak meetings in China."

"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror, precisely these attacks on life," Zelenskyy said.

Skip next section Ukraine death toll rises to 8 after Russian bombardment

Ukraine death toll rises to 8 after Russian bombardment

Ukrainian officials said that the death toll has risen to at least 8 following an overnight Russian aerial bombardment.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said six of the eight people killed were ‌in Kyiv. Two deaths were also reported at a railway station in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 84 cruise missiles in the attack, adding that almost all of them were destroyed.

An unspecified number of ballistic missiles and more than 400 attack drones were also reported to have been destroyed.

Skip next section Poland's defense chief confirms Russian attack on Ukraine 'impacted' Poland

Poland's defense chief confirms Russian attack on Ukraine 'impacted' Poland

Poland's Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said that several Russian flying objects entered Polish airspace during recent air attacks on Ukraine.

"Russian long-range aviation was operating, launching both Kinzhal and Kh-101 missiles, as well as a large number of jet-powered drones and conventional drones. … This Russian Federation attack on Ukrainian territory, which also had an impact on the Republic of Poland, was one of the largest since the beginning of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine," the Defense Ministry quoted Kosiniak-Kamysz as saying.

It comes after Polish prosecutors reported earlier that a flying object had crashed in Poland's eastern Lublin region.

Polish officials said it had taken place during heavy Russian airstrikes on neighbouring Ukraine.

In July, a missile entered Polish airspace and crashed in the same region near the village of Tarnawa Kolonia.

According to the Polish government, it was a Russian CH-101 cruise missile.

Skip next section Poland probing 'violations' of airspace at three locations

Poland probing 'violations' of airspace at three locations

Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that investigations were taking place at three sites after reporting that Polish airspace had been violated.

"In connection with ‌violations ​of Polish airspace, authorities are ​conducting operations at ⁠three ​locations: ​Rudnik nad Sanem, ​Molodycz ‌and Nowy Lipowiec (Lublin ​Province)," ⁠he said in a post on ⁠social ​media platform X.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he had convened a meeting of senior government and military officials along with the heads of security services in a post on X. He said there was currently no danger from the air.

Skip next section WATCH — Ukraine: Premature babies in a war zone

WATCH — Ukraine: Premature babies in a war zone

In war-torn Ukraine, premature babies remain at risk during air raids, while young architects work to save a forgotten gem in Romania.

Skip next section Deaths and damage reported in Russian missile strikes on Kyiv

Deaths and damage reported in Russian missile strikes on Kyiv

Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that a Russian missile bombardment in Kyiv has killed at least three people and injured 13 others.

Klitschko said in a post on Telegram that three bridges had also been damaged following the strikes on Ukraine's capital.

Experts would only be able to give a proper assessment of the damage caused to the structures once the aerial threat had ended, Klitschko added.

"Given the difficult traffic conditions between the left and right banks of the capital, I ask residents not to leave the city by private car unless absolutely necessary," the mayor said.

Klitschko also appealed to employers to allow remote-working arrangements, where possible.

Bridges have been key targets in Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, but Kyiv's forces have managed to hit the Kerch bridge multiple times this week in what is being seen as a major psychological blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

He warned of a harsh response after the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia was struck three times this week.

One of the archways and a section of roadway was destroyed in the attack.

Putin said he expected Moscow's response to be "far more painful" than the damage Ukraine had caused to the Kerch bridge.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Just a day after moves by world leaders to get warring parties to the negotiation table in the form of two summits — one in China, the other in Berlin — Russia has continued with its nightly attacks on Ukraine.

Kyiv has been been targeted by Russian missiles with local officials reporting deaths as a result and damage to at least three bridges.

The latest strikes follow ominous warnings from Russian President Vladimir Putin that Moscow's response would be "far more painful" than the damage done to the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia.

Follow here for the latest updates and analysis from DW's news team.

entries.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
entries.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?
entries.content:
November 20, 2026

German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."

PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Production remains resilient despite decline

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

Analysts call for faster reform

For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

entries.title: COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
entries.summary: After nearly two weeks of negotiations, countries remain divided on how to fight global warming. A new draft declaration doesn't mention the phaseout of fossil fuels, the main drivers of climate change. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026

After nearly two weeks of negotiations, countries remain divided on how to fight global warming. A new draft declaration doesn't mention the phaseout of fossil fuels, the main drivers of climate change. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey

  • A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'

  • Like in previous years, the climate summit is likely to be extended until a consensus is reached

These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20, 2026:

Skip next section 'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration

'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration

The revised draft declaration, which critics have slammed as "watered down" due to the omission of fossil fuels, highlights the "electrification" of the global economy as a central pillar of the energy transition.

"Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen told reporters.

What are the key points to know about the "35-by-35" electrification target?

  • The draft wants to increase electricity's share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035
  • The draft highlights electrification as a way to cut emissions and boost energy security — while omitting prior mentions of fossil fuels
  • It aims to shift more transport, heating, cooling and industrial activity onto electricity, allowing those sectors to be powered by renewables such as wind, solar and hydro power, rather than by burning coal, oil or gas

But the text does not specify what energy sources would supply the electricity. Some countries are demanding that the text call for "clean" electrification to clearly favor renewable sources over coal, oil or gas.

Bowen, who has been trying to secure compromises, pledged to continue working over the "coming hours, for as long as it takes, to get the job done."

"People have strong views of course — I am not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me let's give up and go home," Bowen said.

Skip next section Climate Action Network blames rich nations for 'worst COP ever'

Climate Action Network blames rich nations for 'worst COP ever'

The Climate Action Network (CAN), a global network of over 2,500 civil society organizations, has accused wealthy developed nations, led by the EU, "of blocking every track" towards a substantive agreement on fighting climate change and curbing fossil fuel use.

At its final press conference of the summit, CAN executive director Tasneem Essop said the group was "rejecting what is currently on the table."

"There is nothing (...) that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. The current text has opened the door to the most harmful and dangerous options of any COP so far," Essop said.

She pointed out that this year's COP had the highest ever number of lobbyists for fossil fuels, for AI, for CCUS (Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage) and for CDR (Carbon Dioxide Removal), which only represent corporate interests and do not have the interests of the people from developing nations who are most at risk from global warming in mind.

"What we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to promote the interests of those corporations making profits from the destruction of people," Essop said.

Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa, which is also part of CAN, said: "The COP Presidents want to tell us this has been a great COP. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever.

"Overseeing a failing COP is bad enough, but trying to sell it as a success rubs salt into the wounds of those people who need it to deliver."

Adow cautioned that communities that live with the constant threat of drought, floods and failed harvests were "promised action."

"They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises," Adow said.

He laid the blame squarely with the world's most developed nations: "They demand action from developing countries, then block public finance, block Just Transition, block climate finance, and they expect ambition. You cannot keep your foot on the brake and complain that countries are not moving fast enough."

Skip next section 'Are you serious?' Youth climate activist questions rich nations' commitment

'Are you serious?' Youth climate activist questions rich nations' commitment

Xiye Bastida, a New York-based youth activist from Mexico, spoke to DW's Katharina Schantz to describe her frustration over the lack of progress and ambition on display at this year's COP Summit, which is the seventh the 24-year-old has attended.

Bastida, who has played a leading role in the Fridays for Future climate movement in New York, said she did not think she "could be more disappointed" at how climate targets are "being rolled back."

"This is really the time of reckoning," Bastida said.

She explained that she had changed her flight plans to be able to stay until the end, because she feels "we have to be here. We at least to be witnesses of how they're taking things away."

Bastida pointed to the hypocrisy from wealthy nations, who have blamed some from the Global South for not wanting the summit's joint declaration to mention fossil fuels.

"But they (the Global North) are the ones not bringing the money, and they're the ones who are not bringing the ambition.

"And they want to show themselves as the leaders. But if you want to mention fossil fuels so bad, where's the money for the transition? Where are the roadmaps?

"Are you serious?" Bastida concluded.

Skip next section 'We fear the last couple of weeks will be just a talk show': Sierra Leone spokesperson tells DW

'We fear the last couple of weeks will be just a talk show': Sierra Leone spokesperson tells DW

The new draft declaration, which, as we've reported, has been panned by the EU and civil society, has also disappointed some of the world's least developed countries (LDCs) that are most vulnerable to climate change.

The LDC Group, which comprises 44 of the world's least wealthy nations, came into this year's COP summit hoping for stronger climate action than what has been achieved so far.

"It’s a moment of anticipation," Lamin Sheriff, a press attache for the Sierra Leone government, told DW's Katharina Schantz.

"Ministers from LDCs have requests on the table for the presidency. So whilst they wait on what the outcome would be, everybody is waiting patiently. So the moment is really: we are hopeful for the future, but we are also worried because if proper care is not taken, all what we have debated about here in the last couple of weeks will just be a talk show (…) We can't do anything at the moment."

Skip next section WATCH — Oil interests and climate promises collide at the COP31 summit

WATCH — Oil interests and climate promises collide at the COP31 summit

From clashes over fossil fuels to disputes over climate finance, COP31 exposes the contradictions at the heart of global climate diplomacy.

Climate activist Greta Thunberg says that COP has turned into a "greenwashed circus."

But supporters say the world would be worse off without the COP process.

DW's Tim Schauenberg reports from the summit in Antalya.

Skip next section Summit winding down but negotiators still scrambling for substantive results

Summit winding down but negotiators still scrambling for substantive results

Here's the latest dispatch from DW's Tim Schauenberg, who is in Antalya covering the COP31 summit for us:

"Formally speaking, the final hours of the climate conference have begun. The countries' pavilions have been coming down since Thursday: empty halls, chopped-up timber, lonely lecterns.

Things don't look quite so bleak yet at the negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, and yet, time is running out here. If this is indeed to be, as the COP31 President has already announced, the "best COP ever," the delegations here will have to step up their efforts considerably.

At present, the corridors are buzzing with discussions amongst scientists, NGOs and media representatives. The delegations are doing what they are here to do: negotiating. So, the long wait has begun — not just for a final decision, but also for substance.

Because that is what has been lacking here in Antalya.

Under discussion is a global target to generate 35% of primary energy from electricity by 2035. The EU is determined that this electricity should be generated from solar and wind power. Other countries, particularly those reliant on fossil fuels, want to block the target altogether.

Positions have hardened on this issue — and others — even after two weeks of negotiations. An EU spokesperson is currently making her way through the media center; anyone who doesn't bump into her in the corridors will receive a phone call. The message: the EU will not accept the latest draft of the negotiations as it stands.

This is partly because the issue of carbon capture and storage features prominently in the presidency's latest summary of the negotiations. However, this is expensive and technically complex, and will not halt the climate crisis. Nor is there currently any consensus on turning our backs on the root cause — namely, the burning of coal, oil and gas.

The likelihood that an agreement on this last point will be reached is close to zero, since all 197 countries must agree to this, and Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran and India have no interest in fundamentally questioning their revenue streams and energy plans in the near future.

So the coffee stands are well stocked, and everyone is keeping at least one eye on the flickering screens in the long halls that display all the events on today's agenda. So far, there is a gaping void when it comes to the sessions intended for the press. That could change at any moment — or take hours.

Quite a few media representatives have already brought bags full of provisions with them this morning. They are clearly preparing for a long weekend."

Skip next section Climate NGOs 'firmly reject' COP31 draft declaration

Climate NGOs 'firmly reject' COP31 draft declaration

Climate and social justice activist Harjeet Singh has called on wealthy nations to "stop blocking" efforts to phase out fossil fuels and cut harmful emissions.

In a statement sent to DW reporters at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Singh said, "Civil society firmly rejects this COP31 draft text" which omitted any mention of fossil fuels, despite these being established by scientists as the main causes of climate change.

Singh, Global Convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, also highlighted that the declaration failed to address funding for developing nations that would help them transition away from fossil fuels.

"Our message to rich countries is simple: stop blocking. Put real money on the table for adaptation, for loss and damage, and for developing countries to move away from fossil fuels. And cut your own emissions at home, in line with your fair share. You caused this crisis. You have the money. What you lack is the will, and history will judge you for it," he said.

The draft text, presented on Thursday night, "erases fossil fuels, deletes the money and buries the just transition," Singh said, adding that climate NGOs would not sign it in its current form.

"We call on developing country governments not to sign away their people's survival for a deal that offers workshops instead of finance," he said.

Skip next section EU slams COP31 draft as 'not acceptable'

EU slams COP31 draft as 'not acceptable'

European Union negotiators have told German news agency dpa that the current COP31 draft declaration, which omits any mention of fossil fuels, is "not acceptable," as they aired their frustration with the current state of negotiations.

The summit is formally set to end at 6 p.m. local time (1500 UTC), but it is likely that the deadline will be extended, as it has in previous years.

The draft declaration's main proposal aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from 23% to 35% by encouraging nations to favor cleaner electric alternatives over fossil-fuel-powered cars, heating systems and industrial processes in order to cut emissions.

Some 90 governments, including many EU states, back the proposal, although it is likely to be watered down amid opposition from oil-producing states.

Meanwhile, a number of African countries have said they will only support the electrification target if they receive increased funding to help deal with the impacts of climate change.

Skip next section Turkey to start offshore hydrocarbon drilling next year

Turkey to start offshore hydrocarbon drilling next year

A Turkish seismic research vessel is set to start searching for oil and gas off the coast of Pakistan next year, Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said Friday.

The announcement that Turkey will start drilling offshore for oil and gas resources comes as the country hosts COP31.

"At a time when global oil and natural gas markets are experiencing a historic supply shock, we are bringing the experience we have gained in our own waters and our domestic engineering expertise to our friend and brother, Pakistan," Bayraktar said in a post on X.

Turkey's state oil company ​TPAO signed hydrocarbon exploration and production agreements last year with several ​Pakistani companies for three offshore fields in Pakistan, as well as two onshore fields.

Skip next section WATCH — UN warns climate change could displace millions

WATCH — UN warns climate change could displace millions

Climate-related disasters are uprooting people at an unprecedented rate. From floods in Nepal to droughts, storms and wildfires across the globe, millions are being forced from their homes.

DW speaks with Atle Solberg of the Platform on Disaster Displacement and DW climate correspondent Tim Schauenberg, who was reporting from protests at COP31 in Antalya.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal

IN DEPTH — Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal

One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas.

Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

Learn more about why fossil fuels, the main drivers of global warming, were removed from the COP31 draft declaration in this report.

Skip next section COP summit poised to be extended with no deal imminent

COP summit poised to be extended with no deal imminent

Delegations from nearly 200 countries have been meeting in the Turkish resort city of Antalya since November 9 to negotiate ways to tackle global warming and provide financial aid to the world's poorest and most vulnerable nations to climate change.

But, as in previous years, countries remain sharply divided, and consensus has proven elusive.

Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, nations pledged to move away from fossil fuels, although no target or timeline was ever set.

Oil- and gas-producing countries have strongly resisted attempts to bring that particular issue back to the negotiating table.

Last year's COP30 summit in Brazil concluded with no mention of fossil fuels, prompting some nations to pursue the fight outside of the UN's sphere.

This year's summit is being held against the backdrop of rising living costs and the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has sent shockwaves through global energy markets and sent prices soaring.

Those challenges have taken the focus away from long-standing issues like rising global temperatures and increasingly frequent and extreme weather disasters, which have been exacerbated by this year's record-breaking El Nino.

In an initial draft deal earlier in the week, the phaseout of fossil fuels was included.

But a new draft declaration released on Thursday night by Australia, which is co-hosting the summit, omits any mention of gas, oil and coal, widely recognized as the main drivers of climate change.

The omission is a "black mark," France's Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.

Climate activists have also slammed what they call a "glaring regression."

"You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don't need to phase out fossil fuels," said Harjeet Singh, convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign.

The director of Power Shift Africa, Mohamed Adow, also condemned the slimmed-down draft text, which he said had "gone backwards."

Despite the current differences, Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, said, "We will be consulting and negotiating until it is very clear to us that we have a consensus."

Skip next section IN PICTURES — Hotter seas, more plastic: High stakes for oceans

IN PICTURES — Hotter seas, more plastic: High stakes for oceans

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Have we missed our chance on climate?

IN DEPTH — Have we missed our chance on climate?

From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

Learn more about whether the world is acting too late to stop catastrophic climate change in this report.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Thank you for joining us as we bring you live updates from what is scheduled to be the final day of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey's southern Mediterranean resort city.

Like in previous years, however, it is looking increasingly likely that the negotiations will have to be extended, amid significant differences between delegates despite nearly two weeks of talks.

A new version of a joint draft declaration unveiled on Thursday night omits any mention of how to transition away from fossil fuels — the main causes of global warming.

Stay tuned as we bring you more details on those talks in this blog.

entries.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
entries.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.
entries.content:
November 20, 2026

According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs?

This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

How else is Lufthansa planning to save money?

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.
